_meta.scope: When the asset is a reactor: what commercial structure has actually been signed, by whom, on what terms, and at what published price.
angles_run: build-own-operate + long-term PPA to a single host (Oklo/Eielson, Oklo/Equinix, Oklo/Switch)
reactor-as-a-product: preorders, deposits, reservation fees (Radiant/Equinix, NANO/Supermicro, Last Energy, Deep Fission)
government-as-first-customer vehicles (DIU ANPI, Project Pele, Army Janus, DOE reactor pilot program, INL DOME)
utility ownership and rate-basing (OPG Darlington BWRX-300, TVA, TerraPower/Kemmerer, Utah)
cost-share and risk-sharing instruments (DOE ARDP, X-energy/Dow, 45U/45Y/48E tax credits)
heat rather than electricity (Dow Seadrift, industrial steam)
reactor-only contract terms (decommissioning funding assurance, Price-Anderson tiers, operator licensing, security force, HALEU)
absences: PRIMARY ABSENCE: no contracted $/MWh price for any microreactor (1-20 MW) PPA has ever been published. The only such document filed with a regulator - the Oklo/Equinix letter of intent filed as SEC Exhibit 10.19 - has its price term literally redacted to '####'. Every $/MWh number in circulation for a microreactor is a vendor projection, not a signed price.
Could not verify any dollar value for any Defense Innovation Unit ANPI Other Transaction award; DIU's own announcement states no dollar figures and no ownership model.
Could not verify the value or price terms of the Oklo/Eielson AFB contract; DLA Energy issued only a Notice of Intent to Award, and no executed contract or price appears in any public source.
Could not find a disclosed deposit amount or unit price for the Radiant/Equinix 20-microreactor preorder, the NANO Nuclear/Supermicro arrangement, or any Last Energy customer contract.
Could not find a state utility commission order that has actually approved rate-basing of a microreactor (1-20 MW) - all rate-base precedents found are 300 MW-class SMRs or larger.
Could not verify a published price basis ($/klb steam, $/MMBtu) for the X-energy/Dow Long Mott process-heat offtake; the heat price is not disclosed.
Could not locate a microreactor decommissioning funding assurance amount in an NRC filing; the NRC's certification amounts in 10 CFR 50.75 are keyed to reactor classes far larger than 20 MWe.

Agent terminated on a session limit part-way through. Angles not completed: utility rate-basing of a small reactor, cost-share instruments (ARDP, X-energy/Dow), heat-not-electricity contracts, and the reactor-specific contract terms (decommissioning assurance, Price-Anderson, HALEU).

mechanisms.name: Government build-own-operate plus a long-term PPA to a single installation
mechanisms.what_it_is: A federal agency (here DLA Energy, contracting for the Department of the Air Force) buys energy, not a reactor. The vendor licenses, builds, owns and operates the plant on or adjacent to the installation, and sells electricity and steam to that single host under a long-term power purchase agreement. The government takes no construction risk, no NRC licensing risk and no decommissioning liability; the vendor takes all of it and recovers it in the energy price. Federal agencies have statutory authority (10 U.S.C. 2922a) to sign energy contracts up to 30 years, which is what makes the structure financeable at all.
mechanisms.who_signs: Defense Logistics Agency Energy (for the Department of the Air Force) <-> reactor developer (Oklo Inc.)
mechanisms.term: long-term PPA; DoD energy-contract authority runs to 30 years
mechanisms.price_form: $/MWh plus a heat/steam component, under a firm-fixed-price PPA - never published

precedents.name: Eielson AFB microreactor pilot - first tentative selection
precedents.parties: US Air Force / DLA Energy <-> Oklo Inc.
precedents.size: Aurora powerhouse; electricity plus steam to Eielson AFB, Alaska
precedents.price: not published; contract characterised in press as '$100-million-plus'
precedents.note: STATUS CORRECTION: this award did NOT stand. Ultra Safe Nuclear protested that a contract at or above $100M required discussions and negotiations, and the Air Force revoked the intent to award in late September 2023.

precedents.name: Eielson AFB microreactor pilot - reissued Notice of Intent to Award
precedents.parties: DLA Energy (for the Department of the Air Force) <-> Oklo Inc.
precedents.size: Aurora powerhouse delivering electricity and heat to Eielson AFB, Alaska
precedents.note: Reissued 2025-06-11 after the 2023 rescission. This is a NOITA, not an executed contract: as of this capture no signed agreement, term, capacity or price has been published for it.

mechanisms.nuclear_fit: The structure itself is ordinary - DoD has bought third-party-owned energy on long-term PPAs for solar and cogeneration for years. What nuclear changes is the sequencing: the vendor cannot deliver energy without an NRC licence, so the PPA is signed years before the licence application is filed, and the government is contracting against a permitting risk it cannot itself resolve. It also changes the protest surface: the $100M Federal Acquisition Regulation threshold for required discussions is trivially crossed by a reactor and not by a solar array, which is exactly what killed the first Eielson award.
mechanisms.microreactor_edge: At 1-20 MW the whole plant serves one host, so there is no wholesale market to sell surplus into and no second offtaker to diversify credit risk - the installation IS the market, and the PPA is the entire revenue stream. A 300 MW unit at the same base would have to sell 90% of its output to the grid and therefore needs an interconnection agreement, a transmission study and a utility counterparty; the 1-20 MW unit needs none of those, which is why the microreactor case can be a pure bilateral government PPA and the large-reactor case cannot.
blockers: FAR $100M threshold for required discussions - the basis of the successful Ultra Safe Nuclear protest that voided the 2023 Eielson award
A NOITA is not a contract; no executed Eielson agreement has been published as of 2026-08
NRC licence must be obtained after the PPA is signed, so the offtaker holds schedule risk it cannot price
No published price means no comparator for the next installation to negotiate against

mechanisms.name: Reservation fee plus right of first refusal and most-favoured-nation pricing, ahead of any PPA
mechanisms.what_it_is: A corporate offtaker pays a large cash reservation fee to a pre-revenue developer in exchange for a right of first refusal over a block of future output and a most-favoured-nation pricing guarantee - without signing a PPA, agreeing a price, or naming a site. The fee is not a prepayment for energy: it is returned to the buyer as a discount against future PPA pricing. The buyer is effectively buying an option on capacity and a promise that no later customer gets better terms; the developer is buying non-dilutive cash and a reference customer. Ownership, fuel risk, availability risk and price are all deferred to a PPA that does not yet exist.
mechanisms.who_signs: Hyperscale data-centre operator (Equinix, Inc.) <-> reactor developer (Oklo Inc.)
mechanisms.term: 36-month ROFR window; anticipated PPA term of 20 years, renewable for further 20-year terms
mechanisms.price_form: $/MWh to be set in a future PPA - the price term is REDACTED in the filed exhibit

precedents.name: Equinix - Oklo confidential Letter of Intent to Purchase Power
precedents.parties: Equinix, Inc. <-> Oklo Inc.
precedents.size: approximately 500 MW, stated as 4,380,000 MWh/yr of electric energy output
precedents.price: REDACTED. The filed exhibit replaces every price term with '####'. A $25,000,000 reservation fee is disclosed; the $/MWh is not.
precedents.note: Signed 2024-02-16, filed as Exhibit 10.19 to AltC Acquisition Corp's S-4/A on 2024-04-15. Fee returned as a 10% discount to most-favoured-nation pricing; MFN clause bars Oklo from giving any later customer better terms without offering them to Equinix. 4,380,000 MWh on 500 MW implies a 100% capacity factor, which is itself a negotiating artefact rather than a plant specification.

mechanisms.nuclear_fit: This is what an offtake looks like when the asset cannot be delivered for five to ten years and no unit of it has ever been built. There is no price because there is no cost basis - the first-of-a-kind capex is unknown to both parties. The MFN clause is the tell: the buyer is not protecting a price, it is protecting itself against discovering later that the price was set arbitrarily. A gas or solar offtaker does not need MFN protection because a market clearing price exists.
mechanisms.microreactor_edge: Equinix's 500 MW is an aggregation of many small units, so the ROFR is written over MWh in a fleet rather than over a single plant's output - the LOI expressly contemplates phased deployment across multiple sites with locations named later. That is only possible with factory-built units. A 300 MW reactor is one site, one licence and one in-service date, so the equivalent contract is a single-site PPA with a fixed COD, not a portfolio option. The microreactor's modularity is what turns the offtake into an option on a production line.
blockers: Price term redacted from the public filing - no comparator exists for any subsequent negotiation
MFN clause creates a ratchet: Oklo cannot discount to a later customer without repricing Equinix
ROFR expressly excludes powerhouses supplying any governmental entity and those in Idaho, Ohio and Arizona
LOI is expressly non-binding as to terms - 'intended as a guide in the negotiations and preparation of a PPA'

mechanisms.name: DOE-authorized test reactor under an Other Transaction Agreement, with no federal money and no NRC licence
mechanisms.what_it_is: The developer signs an Other Transaction Agreement with DOE and builds a reactor on its own site with its own capital, authorised under DOE's nuclear safety process rather than an NRC licence. DOE supplies the authorisation pathway (Nuclear Safety Design Agreement, then Preliminary Documented Safety Analysis, then Documented Safety Analysis) and in some cases HALEU fuel; it does not supply construction money. The developer bears 100% of capex and schedule risk in exchange for reaching criticality years earlier than the NRC route allows. A parallel Strategic Partnership Project pathway exists in which a national-lab contractor, not the developer, retains design control.
mechanisms.who_signs: US Department of Energy <-> reactor developer (11 selected projects)
mechanisms.term: milestone-based; the programme's own deadline was criticality by 2026-07-04
mechanisms.price_form: no price - the developer self-funds; DOE contributes authorisation and, for some, fuel

precedents.name: DOE Reactor Pilot Program - initial selections
precedents.parties: DOE <-> Aalo Atomics, Antares Nuclear, Atomic Alchemy, Deep Fission, Last Energy, Natura Resources, Oklo (two projects), Radiant Industries, Terrestrial Energy, Valar Atomics
precedents.size: 11 projects, predominantly microreactor-scale test units
precedents.price: no DOE construction funding disclosed; the instrument conveys authorisation, not cash
precedents.note: Created under Executive Order 14301. Target was criticality for at least three concepts outside the national laboratories by 2026-07-04.

precedents.name: First DOE-authorized criticalities outside the national laboratories
precedents.parties: DOE <-> Antares Nuclear (2026-06-04), Valar Atomics (2026-06-18), Aalo Atomics (2026-07-06)
precedents.size: three test reactors; a fourth developer, Deployable Energy, is also reported critical
precedents.note: STATUS: the programme met its target. DOE's own page lists Antares 2026-06-04 and Valar 2026-06-18 before the 2026-07-04 deadline, Aalo 2026-07-06 just after. Two authorisation pathways are in use: an OTA under which the developer retains design control, and a Strategic Partnership Project under which the lab contractor (Battelle, for Oklo's Pluto) retains it.

mechanisms.nuclear_fit: This is the one mechanism in this file with no non-nuclear analogue at all - it exists because the Atomic Energy Act gives DOE independent authority to authorise reactors on its own terms, so a developer can bypass the NRC entirely for a test unit. The catch is that a DOE-authorized reactor cannot sell power commercially; it buys schedule, not revenue. The design-control question is the commercial crux: under the SPP pathway the developer hands design control to a lab contractor, which is a very different deal from the OTA pathway.
mechanisms.microreactor_edge: Every one of the 11 selected projects is small enough to be built with venture capital rather than project finance - which is the only reason a self-funded, unfunded-by-DOE pathway is usable at all. A 300 MW unit cannot be built on a company balance sheet with no offtake and no federal cost share; a 1-5 MW test unit can. The pathway therefore selects for microreactors by construction, not by policy preference.
blockers: DOE authorisation does not permit commercial power sales - a separate NRC licence is still needed to sell into a host or a grid
No federal construction funding: the developer carries the whole first-of-a-kind capex
Under the Strategic Partnership Project pathway the lab contractor, not the developer, retains design control
Criticality of a test unit is not evidence of a bankable commercial product

mechanisms.name: DoD Other Transaction Authority for commercially owned and operated reactors on an installation
mechanisms.what_it_is: The Defense Innovation Unit runs a Commercial Solutions Opening, screens vendors into an eligible pool, and then awards Other Transactions to selected vendors to design, license, build and operate microreactor plants on named installations. The reactors are commercially owned and operated - the Army buys resilient power, not a reactor - and the awards are structured as fixed-price milestone payments on commercial terms rather than cost reimbursement. The Army executed a Memorandum of Agreement with DIU so it could use DIU's OTA rather than a FAR-based procurement, which is what avoids the protest exposure that voided the first Eielson award.
mechanisms.who_signs: Defense Innovation Unit (under a Memorandum of Agreement with the US Army) <-> selected microreactor vendors
mechanisms.term: prototype OTs with follow-on production authority; EO 14299 sets an operating deadline of 2028-09-30
mechanisms.price_form: fixed-price milestone payments; power price to the installation not disclosed

precedents.name: Advanced Nuclear Power for Installations (ANPI) - eligible vendor pool
precedents.parties: DIU / DoD <-> Antares Nuclear, BWXT Advanced Technologies, General Atomics Electromagnetic Systems, Kairos Power, Oklo, Radiant Industries, Westinghouse Government Services, X-energy
precedents.size: eight vendors; systems sized to meet 100% of an installation's critical loads
precedents.price: NO DOLLAR VALUE DISCLOSED. DIU's own announcement states no award amounts, no ownership model and no capacity range.
precedents.note: Announced 2025-04-10. Selection confers eligibility for Other Transaction awards, not an award.

precedents.name: Army Janus Program - nine named installations
precedents.parties: US Army / DIU <-> vendors to be selected
precedents.size: Fort Benning, Fort Bragg, Fort Campbell, Fort Drum, Fort Hood, Fort Wainwright, Holston Army Ammunition Plant, Joint Base Lewis-McChord, Redstone Arsenal
precedents.price: no dollar figure published
precedents.note: Solicitation via DIU's Commercial Solutions Opening, solution briefs due 2025-12-15. Reactors will be commercially owned and operated, and Army-regulated rather than NRC-licensed. EO 14299 requires an operating Army-regulated reactor by 2028-09-30.

mechanisms.nuclear_fit: The Army-regulated pathway is the structural innovation: a reactor on a federal installation can be authorised by the Army under its own authority instead of by the NRC, which removes the single longest item from the schedule. It also removes the thing a commercial lender underwrites - an NRC licence is an asset, an Army authorisation is not transferable to a civilian site. Any vendor financing a Janus unit is financing an asset whose regulatory basis dies with the contract.
mechanisms.microreactor_edge: Nine installations at once only works if the unit is a product. The programme is explicitly buying 'commercially available dual use microreactor technology' from a pool of eight vendors, which is a supply-chain posture, not a project posture. A 300 MW reactor would be one site, one vendor, one 10-year programme; the microreactor version is a fleet buy with milestone payments and interchangeable suppliers - and a base load of a few tens of MW is exactly what one or two units serve.
blockers: No dollar value has ever been published for any ANPI or Janus Other Transaction
Army-regulated authorisation is not an NRC licence and does not travel to a commercial site
EO 14299's 2028-09-30 deadline is shorter than any microreactor has ever taken from award to operation
Eligibility in the ANPI pool is not an award; as of this capture no ANPI OT value is public

mechanisms.name: Cost-type prime contract for a government-owned transportable reactor
mechanisms.what_it_is: The government contracts a manufacturer on a cost-reimbursement basis to build a reactor that the government owns, and operates it on a federal site under DOE safety oversight rather than an NRC licence. There is no PPA and no price per MWh, because the government is not buying energy - it is buying a machine and a demonstration. All cost overrun risk sits with the government; the vendor is paid its costs. This is the only reactor structure where the published dollar figure is the whole truth, and it is brutal: about $300 million of contract value against 1 to 5 MWe of output.
mechanisms.who_signs: DoD Strategic Capabilities Office <-> BWXT Advanced Technologies LLC
mechanisms.term: roughly two years to build the prototype (award 2022, operation targeted 2026)
mechanisms.price_form: cost-type contract - no energy price at all

precedents.name: Project Pele transportable microreactor prototype
precedents.parties: DoD Strategic Capabilities Office <-> BWXT Advanced Technologies LLC
precedents.size: 1 to 5 MWe, connected to Idaho National Laboratory's microgrid
precedents.price: cost-type contract valued at about $300 million. At 1-5 MWe that is roughly $60,000-$300,000 per kW - one to two orders of magnitude above any commercial generation benchmark, because it buys a first-of-a-kind prototype, not electricity.
precedents.note: Awarded June 2022. Operates at INL's Critical Infrastructure Test Range Complex under the safety oversight of DOE's Idaho Operations Office, not an NRC licence. TRISO fuel delivered to INL December 2025; core manufacturing began 2025.

mechanisms.nuclear_fit: A cost-type contract is what a buyer uses when nobody can price the work - which is precisely the condition of every first-of-a-kind reactor. It is also why this number is so often misused: the $300 million is a prototype development cost, and citing it as a microreactor capex is wrong in the same way that citing an X-plane's cost as an airliner's would be. What it does establish honestly is the floor on what a government pays to get a first unit built when it refuses to transfer risk to a vendor.
mechanisms.microreactor_edge: Transportability is the whole point and it only exists at this scale: Pele is designed to be shipped in commercial containers and moved between sites, which is a capability a 300 MW plant cannot have at any price. The corresponding commercial consequence is that the asset is not tied to a site, so it is not real property, is not rate-basable, and cannot be financed against a site licence - it has to be financed as equipment.
blockers: Government ownership means no PPA, no offtake, no revenue model and no price signal for a commercial buyer
DOE Idaho Operations Office safety oversight is not an NRC licence and does not transfer to a commercial site
$300 million for 1-5 MWe is not a commercial capex and must never be quoted as one

mechanisms.name: National-laboratory test bed access as a staged, cost-shared entry into operation
mechanisms.what_it_is: DOE, through the National Reactor Innovation Center, awards small design-phase grants that buy a developer a slot in a shared, DOE-authorised test facility. The developer still pays for and owns its reactor; DOE supplies the containment structure, the safety-basis process and a fraction of the engineering cost. Awards are staged: a front-end engineering and experiment design phase, then a detailed engineering and experiment planning phase gated on a Preliminary Documented Safety Analysis. It is the cheapest published route from a paper design to a fuelled operating reactor, and the dollar figures are small enough to be startling.
mechanisms.who_signs: DOE Office of Nuclear Energy / NRIC (Idaho National Laboratory) <-> microreactor developers
mechanisms.term: staged phases from 2023 award to first fuelled experiment targeted 2026
mechanisms.price_form: grant-funded design awards; test bed access in kind

precedents.name: DOME front-end engineering and experiment design (FEEED) awards
precedents.parties: DOE <-> Radiant Industries, Ultra Safe Nuclear Corporation, Westinghouse
precedents.size: three microreactor experiment designs for the DOME test bed at INL
precedents.price: $3.9 million total across three developers
precedents.note: Announced 2023-10-23. DOME repurposes the Experimental Breeder Reactor-II containment structure and is capped at 20 MWth per experiment.

precedents.name: DOME detailed engineering and experiment planning (DEEP) phase
precedents.parties: DOE <-> Westinghouse (eVinci, up to 5 MWe), Radiant Industries (Kaleidos, 1.2 MWe design; 3.5 MWth full-scale test unit)
precedents.size: two developers advanced to fuelled-experiment planning
precedents.price: combined $5 million
precedents.note: Announced 2024-11-18. Gated on completing a Preliminary Documented Safety Analysis before fabrication and testing. First fuelled reactor experiment targeted 2026.

mechanisms.nuclear_fit: There is no non-nuclear equivalent because there is no other technology whose first article cannot legally be switched on anywhere. DOME exists to supply the one thing a reactor developer cannot buy commercially: a place where a fuelled reactor may lawfully operate. The awards are tiny relative to reactor capex, which tells you what is actually scarce - not money, but an authorised site.
mechanisms.microreactor_edge: DOME's 20 MWth cap is a hard size gate: it is a microreactor facility by design and a 300 MW SMR cannot use it at all. That asymmetry is the single largest schedule advantage a 1-20 MW unit has - it can reach a fuelled, operating first article inside a shared federal containment for single-digit millions of grant support, while a large SMR's only path to a first article is a full NRC construction permit and operating licence on a bespoke site.
blockers: 20 MWth per-experiment cap excludes anything above microreactor scale
A DOME experiment is not a licensed commercial plant and produces no revenue
Slots are scarce and awarded competitively; two developers hold the first campaigns
No published fee schedule for test bed access, so the true developer cost of a DOME campaign is not public

mechanisms.name: Rate-regulated utility ownership: the reactor goes in the rate base, not into a PPA
mechanisms.what_it_is: A regulated utility - or a Crown corporation under an economic regulator - owns the reactor outright, capitalises it, and recovers construction cost plus an allowed return through regulated rates. There is no offtaker and no price per MWh negotiated with anyone: the counterparty is the entire captive customer base, and the 'contract' is a commission order setting payment amounts. This is the only structure in which a small reactor's full capital cost has ever been published, because rate regulation forces disclosure that a bilateral PPA does not. It is also the structure that puts 100% of construction-cost overrun risk on ratepayers unless the commission disallows it.
mechanisms.who_signs: Regulated utility or Crown generator <-> its economic regulator (Ontario Energy Board; for TVA, its own Board under the TVA Act)
mechanisms.term: 60-year design life recovered over a regulated depreciation schedule
mechanisms.price_form: rate-based - allowed return on capital recovered through regulated payment amounts

precedents.name: Darlington New Nuclear Project (DNNP) - four BWRX-300 units
precedents.parties: Ontario Power Generation <-> Government of Ontario / Ontario Energy Board; Canada Growth Fund and Building Ontario Fund as equity investors
precedents.size: 4 x BWRX-300, up to 1,200 MW total, Darlington, Ontario
precedents.price: CAD 20.9 billion total for all four units. First unit CAD 6.1 billion plus CAD 1.6 billion of shared infrastructure (CAD 7.7 billion for phase one); fourth unit estimated CAD 4.1 billion, about 33% below the first. OPG's projected levelised cost is about 14.9 Canadian cents per kWh over a 60-year life - that is OPG's own projection, not a contracted price. Unit one alone is roughly CAD 20,300 per kW before the shared infrastructure is counted.
precedents.note: THE BEST PUBLIC CAPITAL-COST NUMBER FOR ANY SMALL REACTOR. Crucially, the CAD 20.9 billion is an all-in figure on a basis most projects exclude: OPG states it covers licensing, engineering, procurement, construction, operations readiness, contingency, INTEREST and escalation over the ten-year build. Comparing it to an overnight cost understates it; comparing an overnight cost to it overstates the gap. The contingency exists but its size has not been published. Financing: Canada Growth Fund put in CAD 2 billion for 15% and Building Ontario Fund CAD 1 billion for 7.5%, with OPG remaining majority owner - CAD 3 billion of the CAD 20.9 billion is government equity, explicitly to de-risk the project until private capital will enter.

precedents.name: TVA Clinch River BWRX-300
precedents.parties: Tennessee Valley Authority <-> its own Board; NRC construction permit application docketed 2025
precedents.size: one BWRX-300, roughly 300 MWe, Oak Ridge, Tennessee
precedents.price: No total project cost has been published by TVA. What is public is the incremental development spend its Board has authorised: $200 million approved February 2022 and a further $150 million in April 2024, for $350 million to date on design and development alone - before any construction commitment.
precedents.note: TVA is federally owned and self-financing, so there is no state commission order to disallow a cost overrun and no adversarial rate proceeding in which a total cost has to be defended. A widely cited overnight cost of $17,949/kW in 2024 dollars is an intervenor's reading of TVA filings (David Schlissel, reported by the Southern Alliance for Clean Energy), not a figure TVA has published, and it should be cited that way.

mechanisms.nuclear_fit: Rate-basing is the oldest way to finance a reactor and remains the only one that has actually produced a published all-in number for a small unit. What nuclear changes is who absorbs the overrun: in a PPA the developer eats it, in a rate base the customer does, which is why commissions resist and why the two North American small-reactor rate-base cases are both public or Crown entities (OPG, TVA) rather than investor-owned utilities. Note also that PacifiCorp's route to TerraPower's 345 MWe Natrium unit at Kemmerer is a power purchase agreement, not ownership - and PacifiCorp has not disclosed the price, so even the utility-adjacent case does not yield a number.
mechanisms.microreactor_edge: A 1-20 MW unit is too small to matter to a rate base and too small to justify the proceeding. OPG's CAD 6.1 billion first unit is a project a regulator will spend two years examining; a CAD 60-100 million microreactor is below the threshold at which most commissions open a certificate proceeding at all, and its cost disappears inside a utility's ordinary capital budget. The consequence cuts both ways: the microreactor escapes the prudence review that OPG's unit must survive, and it also never generates the public cost disclosure that review produces - which is exactly why no microreactor capital cost is public and OPG's is.
blockers: No US state commission has approved rate-basing a reactor under 100 MW; every rate-base precedent found is 300 MW-class or larger
OPG's CAD 20.9 billion includes interest and escalation, so it is routinely mis-compared against overnight costs that exclude both
TVA has published no total cost for Clinch River, only $350 million of authorised development spend
PacifiCorp's Natrium offtake is a PPA with an undisclosed price, so the largest US utility-linked small-reactor deal produces no comparator either
Ratepayers, not the developer, carry construction overrun risk in this structure

mechanisms.name: DOE cost-shared cooperative agreement: the government buys down half the first-of-a-kind capex and owns none of it
mechanisms.what_it_is: DOE signs a multi-year cooperative agreement with a developer under which the two sides split total project cost, invoice by invoice, against agreed technical milestones. DOE takes no ownership, no output and no equity; it buys the existence of a first unit. The Energy Policy Act of 2005 sets the default floor - a non-federal share of not less than 50% for demonstration and commercial application activities - and the ARDP funding opportunity applied that floor to every invoice in every year rather than averaging it over the award, which is a materially tighter constraint than a headline 50-50 implies. Because the split is on total project cost, DOE's dollar commitment is a ceiling, not a budget: it only pays out if the developer spends its half first.
mechanisms.who_signs: US Department of Energy (Office of Clean Energy Demonstrations / Office of Nuclear Energy) <-> reactor developer, under a cooperative agreement
mechanisms.term: 6-7 years for the ARDP demonstration awards
mechanisms.price_form: cost share as a percentage of total project cost - no energy price and no DOE offtake

precedents.name: ARDP demonstration awards - TerraPower Natrium and X-energy Xe-100
precedents.parties: DOE <-> TerraPower LLC; DOE <-> X-energy
precedents.size: Natrium, 345 MWe sodium fast reactor with molten-salt storage (boosting to 500 MWe), Kemmerer, Wyoming; Xe-100, four 80 MWe / 200 MWt high-temperature gas units
precedents.price: Initial funding $160 million, $80 million each. DOE's total ARDP commitment was $3.2 billion over seven years subject to appropriations. GAO recorded DOE awarding TerraPower almost $2 billion and X-energy about $1.2 billion, at a 50-50 split of TOTAL PROJECT COST - which implies total project costs of roughly $4 billion and $2.4 billion respectively.
precedents.note: The cost-share schedule is not flat. GAO found TerraPower was to cover 60% of project costs in the FIRST year with DOE covering 40%, reverting to 50-50 for the rest of the term - the developer front-loads its own money, the opposite of the Carbon Free Power Project's front-loaded federal share. Awards were announced October 2020 but not executed until February 2021 (X-energy) and May 2021 (TerraPower).

precedents.name: X-energy ARDP demonstration relocated, then topped up
precedents.parties: DOE <-> X-energy, with Dow added as a sub-awardee under X-energy's ARDP cooperative agreement
precedents.size: four Xe-100 units, 320 MWe / 800 MWt, at Dow's Seadrift site in Calhoun County, Texas
precedents.price: An additional $1 billion of DOE cost-shared funding, bringing total DOE support for the Seadrift project to approximately $2.15 billion.
precedents.note: STATUS CORRECTION: the X-energy ARDP demonstration is no longer in Washington State. GAO's 2022 record - and much writing that still cites it - places the Xe-100 Demonstration at Energy Northwest in Washington. DOE instead made Dow a sub-awardee under X-energy's existing cooperative agreement and the demonstration moved to Texas. As of August 2026 no construction has begun; the NRC construction permit decision is expected in the first half of 2027.

mechanisms.nuclear_fit: A 50% cost share is the only instrument that has moved a first-of-a-kind reactor from paper to a construction site in the United States, and its structural weakness is exactly the thing it is praised for: because DOE pays a percentage of whatever the project costs, a cost overrun is shared rather than absorbed, so neither party has the incentive a fixed-price contract creates. It also does not solve the offtake problem at all - a fully cost-shared reactor still has no customer, which is what killed the one ARDP-adjacent project that had a price.
mechanisms.microreactor_edge: The 50% floor is written as a percentage, so it is technology-neutral and scale-neutral - which quietly disadvantages microreactors twice. First, at $2-4 billion of total project cost a large demonstration can absorb a nine-figure federal award, while a $50-150 million microreactor's 50% is a rounding error to DOE and does not justify the cooperative agreement's administrative load. Second, the developer must fund its half BEFORE invoicing, and for a microreactor firm that means raising the entire unit cost in venture equity anyway - which is why the microreactor cohort ended up in the DOE Reactor Pilot Program's no-money authorisation pathway instead of in ARDP.
blockers: DOE's dollar commitment is 'subject to the availability of future appropriations' - it is a ceiling, not a budget
The non-federal 50% applies to each invoice each year, so a developer that cannot fund its half stops drawing federal money immediately
Percentage cost share shares overruns rather than capping them; nobody holds fixed-price risk
Cost share does not create an offtaker - a fully cost-shared reactor still has no customer
Widely repeated siting facts from the 2021-22 award record are stale: the Xe-100 demonstration is in Texas, not Washington

mechanisms.name: Municipal joint-action subscription against a published target power price
mechanisms.what_it_is: A joint-action agency forms a single-purpose LLC, takes the DOE cost share into it, and then sells subscriptions in the plant's output to its member municipal utilities. Each member commits to a share of capacity and pays its share of cost; the agency publishes a target power price that the subscription is sold against, and members hold off-ramps at defined decision points. This is the only nuclear structure that has ever produced a published, project-specific dollars-per-megawatt-hour figure for a small reactor - and the reason it exists is that municipal boards cannot vote on a subscription without a number. The same transparency is what killed the project.
mechanisms.who_signs: Utah Associated Municipal Power Systems (via Carbon Free Power Project, LLC) <-> its member municipal utilities; separately CFPP LLC <-> DOE
mechanisms.asset_owner: public agency (a special purpose entity wholly owned by the joint-action agency)
mechanisms.term: 10-year DOE award term; subscriptions with member off-ramps at defined economic-competitiveness milestones
mechanisms.price_form: $/MWh target power price, published and revised

precedents.name: Carbon Free Power Project - target power price revision
precedents.parties: UAMPS / CFPP LLC <-> NuScale Power; DOE as cost-share provider
precedents.size: six 77 MWe NuScale modules, 462 MWe, at Idaho National Laboratory
precedents.price: $89 per megawatt hour. THIS IS THE ONLY PUBLISHED TARGET POWER PRICE FOR A SMALL MODULAR REACTOR IN THE UNITED STATES. It was announced in January 2023 as a revision upward from an earlier target in the mid-to-high $50s/MWh, driven by commodity and interest-rate escalation. Note that the plant was also downsized from twelve modules to six between 2020 and 2023, so the price rise and the capacity cut happened together.
precedents.note: STATUS: TERMINATED. On 2023-11-08 UAMPS and NuScale mutually agreed to end the project for lack of subscription. DOE's award was up to $1.4 billion and was structured with a front-loaded federal share - at least 70% for the first four years, 23% over the life of the project - the opposite profile to ARDP. Roughly $232 million had been disbursed at termination.

mechanisms.nuclear_fit: Every other nuclear commercial structure hides its price: the Oklo/Equinix letter of intent has its price term redacted, the Eielson award has no published price, PacifiCorp will not disclose its Natrium PPA price, and Dow says only that it expects its cost of energy net of subsidies to be competitive. CFPP is the exception because a joint-action agency's members are public bodies that vote in public. The lesson is uncomfortable and worth stating plainly: the one small-reactor project that published a price could not sell its output at that price.
mechanisms.microreactor_edge: The subscription model is a way of assembling many small buyers into one large plant - the opposite of the microreactor thesis, which is to put one small plant next to one buyer. At 1-20 MW there is nothing to subscribe: a single host takes the whole output, so there is no committee, no public vote, and correspondingly no published price. That is precisely why the microreactor sector has no price benchmark and the 300 MW-class sector has exactly one.
blockers: The project was terminated in November 2023; $89/MWh is a historical target price, never a delivered one
Target price rose roughly 50% in about two years while the plant shrank from twelve modules to six
Member off-ramps mean subscription can evaporate at each milestone, which is what happened
A front-loaded federal cost share leaves the taxpayer exposed to early termination - DOE had disbursed about $232 million

mechanisms.name: Host-owned reactor selling itself steam: the industrial offtaker becomes the NRC licensee
mechanisms.what_it_is: The industrial host does not buy power from anyone. It creates a wholly owned single-purpose subsidiary, that subsidiary becomes the NRC construction permit applicant and eventual licensee, and the reactor delivers high-pressure steam and electricity across the fence to the parent's own plant. There is no PPA, no third-party developer owning the asset, and therefore no negotiated price at all - the transfer is internal. The vendor's role collapses to technology supply and EPC. This is the structural inverse of the build-own-operate PPA model, and it is what a buyer chooses when the product is process heat rather than electricity, because heat cannot be wheeled and has no market price.
mechanisms.who_signs: Dow Inc. (via wholly owned subsidiary Long Mott Energy, LLC) <-> X-energy as reactor supplier; Long Mott Energy <-> NRC as licence applicant
mechanisms.term: no offtake term - the asset is owned by the consumer of its output
mechanisms.price_form: NO PRICE. The output is transferred internally; Dow states only that it expects its cost of energy net of subsidies to be competitive with other firm clean energy.

precedents.name: Long Mott Generating Station construction permit application
precedents.parties: Long Mott Energy, LLC (wholly owned subsidiary of The Dow Chemical Company) <-> US NRC; X-energy as Xe-100 supplier and ARDP prime
precedents.size: four Xe-100 high-temperature gas-cooled units, 800 MWt total / 320 MWe, each unit rated 200 MWt of high-pressure, high-temperature steam, at Dow's UCC Seadrift Operations, Calhoun County, Texas
precedents.price: NO PRICE OR PRICE BASIS IS PUBLISHED - not $/MWh, not $/klb of steam, not $/MMBtu. Dow's only quantitative statement about cost is that it expects the cost of energy, net of all subsidies, to be competitive with other alternatives for firm, clean energy.
precedents.note: Filed 2025-03-31 under section 103 of the Atomic Energy Act and 10 CFR Part 50; NRC Docket No. 99902117, Docket ID NRC-2025-0079, application package ADAMS ML25090A057. First NRC review of the Xe-100 design. The application includes a separate financial qualification submission (ADAMS ML25090A059). The plant replaces existing energy and steam assets at Seadrift that are near end-of-life - so the true comparator is the avoided cost of rebuilding gas-fired cogeneration, which Dow has not disclosed either. As of August 2026 construction has not begun and the permit decision is expected in the first half of 2027.

mechanisms.nuclear_fit: Heat changes the contract, not just the product. Electricity has a market price, a wholesale node and a settlement convention; industrial steam has none of those, so a steam deal has to invent its own price basis - usually indexed to the gas price of the boiler it replaces, plus a fixed capacity charge. When the asset is nuclear, the host has a further reason to own rather than buy: the reactor must sit inside the fence to deliver steam at all, so the host is accepting the reactor's siting, security and emergency-planning footprint on its own site regardless of who owns it. Once you have accepted the footprint, third-party ownership buys you much less than it does for a solar farm across the road.
mechanisms.microreactor_edge: Dow's four-unit plant is 800 MWt because a large petrochemical complex has an enormous steam load; a 1-20 MW microreactor's thermal output is a few tens of MWt at most, which suits a food-processing plant, a district heat loop, a mine's process circuit or a campus - not a cracker. The commercially decisive difference is the licensee: Dow could afford to stand up a subsidiary, a nuclear organisation and a Part 50 application because it is spreading that overhead across 800 MWt. A single 15 MWt host cannot, which forces the microreactor back into a third-party-owned model where the vendor holds the licence and sells heat - a structure for which no signed, priced precedent exists.
blockers: No published price basis of any kind for nuclear process heat - not $/klb steam, not $/MMBtu, not a gas-index formula
Host ownership means the industrial company must become an NRC licensee and build a nuclear operating organisation
The Xe-100 has never been reviewed by the NRC before; Long Mott is the first application of the design
Steam cannot be wheeled, so there is no alternative buyer and no residual value if the host's plant closes
Construction had not begun as of August 2026; permit decision expected first half of 2027

mechanisms.name: Price-Anderson financial protection: a mandatory contract term, priced by reactor size in the regulation itself
mechanisms.what_it_is: Every NRC power reactor licensee must carry financial protection against public liability, and must sign an indemnity agreement with the Commission. This is not background regulation - it is a term the licensee executes, an insurance premium it pays annually, and a contingent liability it must disclose to lenders and to any offtaker doing diligence. The size of the obligation is set in 10 CFR Part 140 as a step function of reactor size, and the steps are enormous. Crucially, the top tier - a $500 million primary layer plus mandatory participation in the industry retrospective pool - attaches only to reactors rated 100,000 electrical kilowatts or more. Everything smaller sits in a much cheaper regime.
mechanisms.who_signs: NRC licensee <-> US Nuclear Regulatory Commission (indemnity agreement under section 170 of the Atomic Energy Act), plus the licensee <-> nuclear liability insurer
mechanisms.asset_owner: third-party developer | utility | host - applies to whoever holds the licence
mechanisms.term: for the life of the licence; the indemnity agreement runs with it
mechanisms.price_form: annual insurance premium plus a contingent deferred premium assessed only after an incident

precedents.name: 10 CFR 140.11(a)(4) - reactors of 100,000 electrical kilowatts or more
precedents.parties: NRC <-> every large power reactor licensee
precedents.size: any power reactor rated at or above 100 MWe
precedents.price: $500,000,000 of primary financial protection PLUS mandatory participation in the industry retrospective rating plan. The deferred premium is capped at $158,026,000 per reactor per nuclear incident, payable at no more than $24,714,000 per incident within one calendar year. Multi-unit sites of 100-300 MWe units totalling no more than 1,300,000 electrical kilowatts count as a single reactor for this assessment.
precedents.note: The retrospective premium is the real liability: it is a several, contingent obligation to pay up to $158 million per reactor after somebody else's accident. It has to be disclosed, and it prices into a lender's covenants.

precedents.name: 10 CFR 140.11(a)(1)-(3) and 10 CFR 140.12 - everything below 100 MWe
precedents.parties: NRC <-> small and micro reactor licensees
precedents.size: reactors up to 10 MWt by fixed tier, and above 10 MWt but below 100 MWe by formula
precedents.price: $1,000,000 at or below 10 kWt; $1,500,000 above 10 kWt to 1 MWt; $2,500,000 above 1 MWt to 10 MWt. Above that and below 100 MWe, 10 CFR 140.12 sets financial protection at $185 per thermal kilowatt multiplied by a population factor of 1.0 to 2.0, subject to a hard floor of $4,500,000 and a hard ceiling of $74,000,000.
precedents.note: Worked example for a microreactor: a 20 MWt unit gives a base of $185 x 20,000 kWt = $3.7 million; even at the maximum population factor of 2.0 that is $7.4 million, and at the minimum population factor the $4,500,000 floor binds. The population factor is computed over minor civil divisions inside a circle whose radius in miles equals the square root of the thermal rating in MW - for a 20 MWt unit that circle is about 4.5 miles, which is why a remote site lands at factor 1.0.

mechanisms.nuclear_fit: There is no analogue in a gas or solar contract. A solar developer carries commercial general liability; a reactor licensee signs a federal indemnity agreement, buys a statutorily specified layer of nuclear liability insurance, and - above 100 MWe - accepts a several contingent obligation for other operators' accidents. For an offtaker's diligence this is the clearest example of a term that exists only because the asset is nuclear, and it is one of the few such terms with an exact published dollar amount rather than a qualitative requirement.
mechanisms.microreactor_edge: This is the sharpest quantitative 1-20 MW versus 300 MW distinction in the whole file, and it runs in the microreactor's favour by two orders of magnitude. A 300 MWe unit must carry $500,000,000 of primary protection and accept a contingent $158,026,000 retrospective assessment. A 20 MWt microreactor is not in that tier at all: its required protection is the 10 CFR 140.12 formula amount, floored at $4,500,000 and capped at $74,000,000, and it is not assessed the deferred premium because the retrospective plan applies to reactors of 100,000 electrical kilowatts or more. A microreactor's Price-Anderson obligation is roughly 1% of a large reactor's, set by a formula in the regulation rather than by negotiation.
blockers: The 10 CFR 140.12 population factor is computed from Census minor civil divisions, so an urban or campus site is penalised up to 2x relative to a remote one
The $4,500,000 floor binds for any microreactor below about 24 MWt at population factor 1.0, so the smallest units get no further reduction for being smaller
Whether a sub-100 MWe licensee can DRAW on the industry secondary layer it does not pay into was not verified in this pass - only that it is not assessed
The dollar figures are periodically adjusted for inflation, so any number quoted in a contract must name its CFR edition

mechanisms.name: The obligations a reactor deal must fund that a gas or solar deal never mentions
mechanisms.what_it_is: Before a reactor can sell a single MWh it must have funded or committed to a set of obligations with no counterpart in a gas or solar contract: a certified decommissioning fund sized by regulation rather than by engineering, NRC-licensed operators on shift, an armed physical protection programme, and material control and accounting. Each is a cost line an offtaker's diligence will find and a lender will size a reserve against. The decommissioning obligation is the one that does not scale: the 10 CFR 50.75 table sets a floor by using a substituted power level for any reactor below 1200 MWt, so a small reactor is charged as if it were a 1200 MWt one. The NRC has proposed a separate framework, Part 57, that would relieve several of these for microreactors - but it is a proposed rule, not law.
mechanisms.who_signs: NRC licensee <-> US NRC; and the licensee <-> a trustee holding the decommissioning fund
mechanisms.asset_owner: third-party developer | utility | host - applies to whoever holds the licence
mechanisms.term: funded before or during operation; the decommissioning certification is filed with the licence application and adjusted annually
mechanisms.price_form: no price - these are cost obligations that must be recovered inside whatever price is charged

precedents.name: 10 CFR 50.75(c)(1) minimum decommissioning funding - the floor that does not scale down
precedents.parties: NRC <-> every power reactor licensee and combined licence applicant
precedents.size: applies to all power reactors regardless of size
precedents.price: In January 1986 dollars: a PWR at or above 3400 MWt must certify $105 million; between 1200 and 3400 MWt the formula is $(75 + 0.0088P) where P is thermal megawatts. THE CRITICAL CLAUSE: 'For a PWR of less than 1200 MWt, use P = 1200 MWt.' So a 20 MWt microreactor certifies the same $85.56 million (1986 dollars) as a 1200 MWt plant - 60 times its thermal rating. For a BWR the formula is $(104 + 0.009P) with the same substitution, giving $114.8 million. The certified amount must then be escalated annually by a factor at least equal to 0.65L + 0.13E + 0.22B, where L and E are Bureau of Labor Statistics labour and energy escalators and B is the waste burial escalator from NUREG-1307.
precedents.note: Two further points that matter commercially. First, the table lists only PWRs and BWRs - a high-temperature gas, sodium-cooled or heat-pipe microreactor is not in it at all, so its amount has to come from a site-specific estimate rather than the table, which removes the certainty the table was meant to provide. Second, 50.75(a) expressly notes that decommissioning funding may also be regulated by FERC or a state PUC with rate jurisdiction, and that the NRC amount is additional to, not a substitute for, those requirements.

precedents.name: Proposed 10 CFR Part 57 - Licensing Requirements for Microreactors and Other Reactors With Comparable Risk Profiles
precedents.parties: NRC <-> future microreactor licensees; Docket ID NRC-2025-0379, proposed rule published 2026-05-01
precedents.size: microreactors and reactors of comparable risk profile; explicitly aimed at high-volume deployment
precedents.price: No dollar figures. The relief is in obligations, not payments: no emergency planning zone would be defined for a Part 57 facility; force-on-force exercises would not be required; reactor operators could hold a general licence with the facility licensee, not the NRC, administering the initial examination; a general licence would cover certain construction activities before a construction permit is issued for an nth-of-a-kind design; and a single joint application would yield the construction permit and the associated operating licence(s) without further prior notice once construction is found substantially complete.
precedents.note: On Price-Anderson the NRC did NOT propose a reduced number. It says it considered reducing the required financial protection for Part 57 facilities and would instead decide case by case on review of a joint application, using the Act's factors - cost and terms of private insurance; type, size and location; and nature and purpose of the activity - and could likewise consider reduced indemnification fees. So the single largest reactor-specific liability term remains, for now, discretionary and unpriced. This is a PROPOSED rule; nothing in it is in force.

mechanisms.nuclear_fit: These are the terms that make a reactor offtake diligence longer than a gas offtake's. A gas plant has a decommissioning obligation measured in demolition cost; a reactor has a federally certified fund whose minimum is set by a table. A solar farm has a fence; a reactor has an armed response force, insider mitigation, vehicle searches and material control and accounting. A CCGT has NERC-qualified operators; a reactor has NRC-licensed operators on shift, and until Part 57 the NRC itself administers the examination. Every one of these is a fixed annual cost that does not shrink with plant size, which is why they dominate a small reactor's operating cost per MWh and are nearly invisible in a large one's.
mechanisms.microreactor_edge: The decommissioning rule is the clearest case in US nuclear regulation of a requirement that is size-blind by construction: the instruction to substitute P = 1200 MWt for any smaller PWR means a 20 MWt unit and a 1200 MWt unit certify the identical amount. On plausible microreactor capital costs that certified fund is of the same order as the plant itself, which is a financing problem no 300 MW unit has. Part 57 is the regulator's answer and it is aimed squarely at this scale - no EPZ, no force-on-force, general-licensed operators, a general construction licence for nth-of-a-kind units, one joint application instead of two proceedings - but it is proposed, so every microreactor deal signed today is priced against the Part 50 obligations, not the Part 57 ones.
blockers: 10 CFR 50.75(c)(1) forces a sub-1200 MWt reactor to certify a 1200 MWt reactor's decommissioning amount
The 50.75(c)(1) table covers only PWRs and BWRs, so non-water microreactors fall outside it and must produce a site-specific estimate
Part 57 is a proposed rule published 2026-05-01; it confers nothing on a deal signed now
Part 57 declines to set a reduced Price-Anderson financial protection amount, leaving it to case-by-case NRC discretion
Decommissioning funding may separately be regulated by FERC or a state PUC; the NRC amount is additional, not substitutive

sources.quote: funds will be available for the decommissioning process

sources.quote: An emergency planning zone (EPZ) would not be defined for facilities licensed under proposed part 57.

mechanisms.name: The technology-neutral tax credits as the only published, contractible price support for a new reactor
mechanisms.what_it_is: A new reactor elects either the section 45Y clean electricity production credit, paid per kilowatt-hour generated for ten years, or the section 48E investment credit, taken as a percentage of qualified investment in the year the plant is placed in service. These are the only dollar figures in the whole nuclear stack that are published, indexed, and knowable in advance, which is why every unpriced deal in this file - Oklo/Equinix, Eielson, Dow, PacifiCorp/Natrium - is quietly negotiated around them. They are also transferable and elective for cash under the IRA machinery, so they function as a financing instrument, not merely a tax attribute. The credits carry conditions that reach directly into the contract: 45Y is available on electricity sold to an UNRELATED person, or on electricity consumed or stored only where the facility has a metering device owned and operated by an unrelated person.
mechanisms.who_signs: Reactor owner <-> US Treasury/IRS; and, where the credit is monetised, the owner <-> a tax-credit transferee
mechanisms.asset_owner: third-party developer | utility | host - follows whoever owns the facility
mechanisms.term: 45Y runs 10 years from placed-in-service; construction must begin before 2034, after which the credits phase out over three years

precedents.name: Section 45Y applicable amounts for calendar year 2025
precedents.parties: IRS / Treasury <-> any qualified clean electricity facility, nuclear included
precedents.size: per kilowatt-hour of qualifying generation
precedents.price: 0.6 cents per kWh base, and 3 cents per kWh ($30/MWh) for a facility meeting prevailing wage and apprenticeship requirements. The 2025 inflation adjustment factor is 1.9971, derived from the GDP implicit price deflator for 2024 (125.234) over 1992 (62.707) - the statutory 0.3 and 1.5 cent amounts have almost exactly doubled since enactment. Published at 90 FR 41477 on 2025-08-25.
precedents.note: SCALE CHECK: $30/MWh against the only published small-reactor target power price in the United States - the Carbon Free Power Project's $89/MWh - is about a third of the price. The credit is large enough to decide whether a project clears, and it is the one number in a nuclear pro forma that is not a projection.

precedents.name: Section 48E investment credit and the OBBBA nuclear energy community adder
precedents.parties: IRS / Treasury <-> facility owner
precedents.size: percentage of qualified investment in the facility
precedents.price: 6 percent of the qualified investment as the base amount, multiplied by five to up to 30 percent where prevailing wage and registered apprenticeship requirements are met, plus 10 percentage points for domestic content in steel, iron and manufactured products, plus 10 percentage points for an energy community. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act added a further nuclear-specific adder of 10% (or two percentage points without prevailing wage and apprenticeship) for an advanced nuclear facility in a metropolitan statistical area with at least 0.17% direct nuclear-related employment at any time since 2010.
precedents.note: The nuclear energy community adder is available ONLY against 45Y, not 48E - so a developer choosing the investment credit forfeits the one credit provision written specifically for nuclear. That makes the 45Y-versus-48E election a genuine structuring decision rather than a modelling preference, and it pushes a nuclear project toward the production credit if its site qualifies.

mechanisms.nuclear_fit: The credits are technology-neutral, which for nuclear is both the enabling fact and the trap. Enabling, because a reactor qualifies on the same terms as a wind farm and needs no bespoke legislation. Trap, because the 45Y unrelated-person condition is written for a merchant generator selling into a market, and the entire microreactor thesis is behind-the-meter sale to a single host - sometimes, as at Dow's Long Mott, to the owner itself. In that configuration the credit survives only through the metering-device route, where the meter is owned and operated by an unrelated person, so a term about who owns a meter becomes a condition of a nine-figure tax position.
mechanisms.microreactor_edge: The election runs opposite ways at the two scales, and the reason is capacity factor and capex intensity. 45Y pays on output, so it rewards a plant that runs; 48E pays on investment, so it rewards a plant that costs a lot per kW. A first-of-a-kind microreactor is extraordinarily capex-intensive per kW and has an unproven capacity factor, which argues for 48E - but taking 48E forfeits the nuclear energy community adder and delivers nothing if the unit is not placed in service. A 300 MW unit at a former nuclear or fossil site has the site qualification, the scale to certify prevailing wage and apprenticeship compliance, and a credible capacity factor, so it can take 45Y at 3 cents/kWh with the nuclear adder on top. The credit regime, without intending to, is better fitted to the large unit.
blockers: 45Y requires sale to an unrelated person, or an unrelated-person-owned metering device for self-consumed power - a direct problem for behind-the-meter and host-owned microreactors
The nuclear energy community adder applies only under 45Y, so electing 48E forfeits the only nuclear-specific credit provision
Construction must begin before 2034, after which the credits phase out over three years - a hard deadline for a technology whose first commercial units are not yet licensed
The 0.17% nuclear-employment community test is keyed to metropolitan statistical areas, which excludes exactly the remote sites microreactors are marketed for
Foreign entity of concern restrictions apply to 45Y and 48E and were not examined in this pass
